sections.guidingQuestion: Why can phospholipids form a stable boundary without an assembly machine?
sections.explanation:
A phospholipid has a polar, water-attracting head and nonpolar hydrocarbon tails that interact poorly with water. Such a molecule is amphipathic: one part is hydrophilic and the other hydrophobic. In an aqueous environment many phospholipids rearrange because exposed tails disrupt favourable interactions among surrounding water molecules.

A bilayer places the heads against the aqueous solutions on both faces and packs the tails inward, away from water. The two layers form a continuous flexible sheet; where a free edge exposes tails, the sheet tends to reseal or curve into an enclosed vesicle. The membrane is a dynamic assembly held together largely by the hydrophobic effect and noncovalent interactions, not by covalent bonds between every lipid.

A synthetic phospholipid vesicle can enclose an aqueous solution even without membrane proteins. This makes a useful model for the lipid foundation of cell boundaries, but a real cell membrane additionally contains diverse proteins and other lipids.

Phospholipid head groups interact with water while the nonpolar fatty-acid tails make contact with one another in the bilayer interior. Bilayer self-assembly is energetically favored because the hydrophobic regions have less contact with surrounding water. A flat bilayer with exposed edges is unfavorable, so a small patch can bend into a closed vesicle. This organization also explains why the outer face and cytosolic face both present hydrophilic head groups. Membranes are not rigid tiles: lipid molecules can move laterally within a leaflet, while movement from one leaflet to the other is much rarer without specialized proteins. This fluid barrier is the foundation on which selective transport proteins operate.

terms: Amphipathic: containing hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions
Bilayer: two opposing leaflets of lipids
Hydrophobic effect: tendency of nonpolar groups to reduce contact with water

sections.guidingQuestion: Why can cells keep chemically different solutions on opposite sides of a thin membrane?
sections.explanation:
The packed hydrocarbon chains create an energetically unfavourable region for many charged and strongly polar solutes. An ion surrounded by water would have to lose much of its hydration shell to enter this region; large polar molecules also cross extremely slowly.

A lipid bilayer therefore separates the cytosol from an external or organelle solution while still allowing some small uncharged molecules through. This selective barrier is essential: without it cells could not sustain different ion concentrations or create many of the gradients used to do biological work.

A salt solution inside a protein-free vesicle can remain chemically distinct from the surrounding water. The barrier is not perfectly impermeable: permeability depends on molecular properties and time, and biological membranes include transport proteins.

In water, ions such as Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are stabilized by hydration shells of oriented water molecules. To cross the nonpolar core of a pure phospholipid bilayer, an ion would need to leave much of that favorable aqueous environment, which imposes a high energy cost. Consequently a bilayer blocks rapid free ion passage even though it is only a few nanometers thick. Ion channels and carriers provide more favorable interactions along specific pathways, allowing controlled movement. The restriction is selective rather than absolute: small nonpolar molecules commonly pass more readily than charged or large highly polar solutes. This helps cells maintain pH, ion concentrations and membrane electrical potential.

sections.guidingQuestion: How do oxygen and carbon dioxide cross a membrane without a carrier or ATP?
sections.explanation:
Oxygen and carbon dioxide are small molecules that can dissolve sufficiently in the bilayer interior to pass between phospholipids. They move by random thermal motion; no individual molecule is directed deliberately toward the less concentrated side.

If more molecules are available on one side, statistically more move from that side to the other per unit time than travel back. The result is net diffusion down a concentration gradient. When concentrations become equal, molecules keep moving in both directions, but there is no net flux.

Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air toward oxygen-poor blood cells and across their plasma membranes. Diffusion rate depends on gradient, available surface area, diffusion distance and the permeant molecule's properties.

Oxygen and carbon dioxide molecules move randomly and can partition into a lipid bilayer. When oxygen concentration is higher on one side, more molecules cross from that side per unit time, so there is a net flux down the concentration gradient. Molecules still move in both directions after the concentrations become equal; dynamic equilibrium means the opposing average rates balance, not that all molecular movement stops. Diffusion requires no direct ATP input, but cells may maintain gradients by metabolism, blood flow or gas exchange elsewhere. Flux also depends on exposed area, membrane properties and diffusion distance, which explains why a larger concentration gradient alone does not fully determine a tissue's gas-exchange performance.

sections.guidingQuestion: How does a lipid boundary host recognition, enzymes, and transport proteins?
sections.explanation:
Proteins in membranes differ in location and form. An integral protein penetrates at least part of the lipid bilayer; many span it fully using hydrophobic amino acid regions that interact with lipid tails. A peripheral protein attaches to one membrane face, often through noncovalent interactions with another protein or polar headgroups.

An integral channel can create a hydrophilic path for selected ions; a membrane receptor can bind an external signalling molecule; and a peripheral protein may help connect the membrane to the cytoskeleton or participate in signalling. Location and molecular shape determine what each protein can do.

In a red blood cell, membrane-spanning transport proteins and peripheral cytoskeletal linkers cooperate to allow exchange while supporting membrane resilience. Not every integral protein is a channel, and not every peripheral protein is outside the cell.

An integral membrane protein is embedded in the bilayer, and a transmembrane protein spans it. Such proteins can create passageways, bind ligands on one side and transmit information across the membrane, or attach the cytoskeleton to an extracellular partner. Peripheral proteins contact one side of the membrane without traversing the entire lipid core. Different domains of the same protein may face chemically different environments: hydrophobic amino-acid residues favor the bilayer interior, while charged regions can contact cytosol or extracellular fluid. A glycoprotein typically displays carbohydrate groups on the noncytosolic face. Structural position helps predict function, but the word 'protein' alone cannot establish whether it forms a channel, receptor, enzyme or anchor.

sections.guidingQuestion: What predicts whether a cell gains or loses water across a selectively permeable membrane?
sections.explanation:
Water molecules move randomly across a cell membrane, both directly through the lipid bilayer and rapidly through aquaporin channels when present. Osmosis describes a net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane when conditions on either side differ.

In a simplified pair of solutions separated by a membrane permeable to water but not a specified solute, the side with more impermeant dissolved solute has lower water potential and tends to receive net water, all else equal. Water moves both ways; the net flux results from an imbalance in the opposing flows. Hydrostatic pressure and permeant solutes can alter a real system.

An animal cell placed in a solution with a lower effective nonpenetrating solute concentration than its cytosol tends to swell. Aquaporins increase water permeability; they do not 'pump' water against its thermodynamic gradient using ATP.

Water crosses biological membranes both through the lipid bilayer and through aquaporin channels. sections.guidingQuestion: How can one ion cross rapidly while another is excluded?
sections.explanation:
An open ion channel forms a hydrated pathway through a membrane's nonpolar interior. The channel's pore geometry and charged or polar residues help favour certain ions over others. Specificity is not simply a matter of an arbitrary hole being large enough.

Ions move through open channels passively down their electrochemical gradients: both the concentration difference and voltage across the membrane can contribute. Opening and closing a channel changes permeability without changing the direction of the ion's driving force by itself.

In neurons, K+ channels can allow K+ to move when their gates are open under a favourable electrochemical gradient. Channel-mediated transport is facilitated diffusion, not energy-coupled pumping.

A channel protein presents an aqueous pathway through the hydrophobic membrane and can discriminate among ions using pore geometry and chemical interactions. A potassium-selective channel, for example, does not simply admit every ion smaller than potassium; its selectivity filter and hydration energetics matter. Opening and closing can regulate when the route is available, but an open passive channel does not consume ATP for each ion passing through. The direction of net ion movement follows its electrochemical gradient, which combines the chemical concentration difference and electrical potential. A change in membrane voltage can therefore alter both the channel's gating and the driving force acting on a permeating ion.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can a membrane protein move a solute against its gradient?
sections.explanation:
To accumulate a solute where it is already abundant, a cell must couple transport to energy. Many pump proteins bind specific particles and change conformation after ATP hydrolysis and associated protein-state changes. The ordered cycle allows transport against a concentration or electrochemical gradient.

The pump must be distinguished from an open pore. A pore would let particles diffuse downhill; a pump undergoes cycles in which access to binding sites alternates between the two sides. Energy supports a direction that would not persist by passive movement alone.

Plant plasma-membrane H+-ATPases use ATP to export protons, building gradients used by other transport processes. Pump specificity means an ATP-powered protein is not a generic conduit for all ions.

Primary active transport couples a protein's conformational cycle directly to an energy source, frequently ATP hydrolysis, so a solute can move against its electrochemical gradient. The protein usually alternates which side of the membrane has access to the bound solute, avoiding a continuous unrestricted pore across the bilayer. Proton ATPases in plant plasma membranes, for example, drive H⁺ outward, helping establish a proton-motive force. That gradient can subsequently drive uptake of other substances through secondary transporters. The words 'active' and 'facilitated' identify different energetic relationships; a transporter that only permits downhill flux is not a pump even if it changes shape during movement.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why is a membrane neither a perfect wall nor a universal filter?
sections.explanation:
Simple diffusion through phospholipids is governed by molecular features, especially size and polarity or charge, rather than recognition by a binding site. Small hydrophobic molecules tend to permeate readily; ions and many large hydrophilic molecules require specialized pathways.

Selective proteins can provide extra routes. A channel permits some ions but not others; a carrier recognizes a substrate and changes shape; a pump can use energy to build gradients. Together, bilayer chemistry and proteins make a membrane selectively permeable.

Two molecules of similar size can cross at very different rates if one is charged and the other nonpolar. Predicting permeability therefore requires identifying the molecular species and which functional transport proteins are present.

To predict transport, start with a molecule's size, polarity, charge and potential interactions with lipids. Small nonpolar gases such as oxygen can diffuse through the bilayer more readily than ions; water moves slowly through the lipid portion and often more rapidly through aquaporins. Large charged molecules generally need specialized pathways or vesicular traffic. Transport proteins introduce selectivity and regulated access, so two similarly sized molecules can cross at very different rates. Conditions also matter: membrane composition, temperature, protein expression and concentration differences affect measured flux. Avoid an absolute ranking that assumes every membrane contains the same channels or that all solutes move only from a high concentration to a low concentration.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can the outside of a cell display a molecular identity?
sections.explanation:
Many membrane proteins and lipids carry short or branched carbohydrate chains. A glycoprotein contains a covalently attached carbohydrate on a protein; a glycolipid bears carbohydrate on a lipid. For plasma membranes, these carbohydrate moieties generally project on the extracellular surface.

Surface carbohydrates contribute to molecular recognition and adhesion. Their differing sugar sequences and arrangements can influence which cell-associated proteins or neighbouring cells interact. Specific adhesion often requires specialized binding proteins rather than sugars alone.

The ABO blood-group antigens are carbohydrate structures displayed on red-cell surface molecules, providing a concrete example of recognition. A diagram should not place these glycans projecting from the cytosolic face of the plasma membrane.

Carbohydrate chains attached to membrane proteins and lipids usually face the extracellular fluid or the lumen of internal secretory compartments. When a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, its luminal face becomes continuous with the extracellular-facing surface; the membrane does not turn inside out. This topology explains how glycosylated groups can function in cell recognition, adhesion and communication. Blood-group antigens are one example of exposed sugar patterns that can be recognized differently by antibodies. Sugar chains are not normally drawn protruding into both cytosol and extracellular space. Their orientation is biologically meaningful and must be preserved in membrane and exocytosis diagrams.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can you draw a membrane that conveys both structure and movement?
sections.explanation:
The fluid mosaic model describes proteins embedded in or attached to a laterally mobile lipid bilayer. The hydrophilic phosphate heads contact water, and the nonpolar tails face inward. Integral proteins intersect the lipid matrix; peripheral proteins attach to one face.

An accurate two-dimensional diagram for this understanding should label phospholipids, hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions, an integral protein, a peripheral protein, extracellular carbohydrate on a glycoprotein, and cholesterol positioned among hydrocarbon tails. Not every lipid or protein moves freely: the cytoskeleton and interactions can restrict mobility.

Fluid does not mean membranes dissolve or become random soup. The bilayer remains an organized barrier while components move or reorganize on biologically relevant timescales.

The fluid-mosaic model describes a dynamic phospholipid matrix containing many kinds of integral and peripheral proteins. Cholesterol in many animal membranes lies with its small hydroxyl group close to the polar head region and its fused nonpolar rings among hydrocarbon tails. Some proteins and lipids are concentrated in particular regions or anchored to the cytoskeleton, so mobility does not imply completely uniform distribution. A good drawing places glycoprotein carbohydrate chains on the noncytosolic face, channels spanning the bilayer and peripheral proteins associated with a face rather than buried as full transmembrane pores. Selective transport and signal recognition emerge from that chemical and spatial organization.

sections.guidingQuestion: Why might organisms adjust membrane lipids as their habitat cools?
sections.explanation:
Saturated hydrocarbon tails pack relatively tightly, whereas cis double bonds in unsaturated tails introduce bends that disrupt close packing. Lipids with more unsaturated fatty acids generally have lower melting or phase-transition temperatures than otherwise comparable saturated lipids.

At low temperatures, increasing the proportion of unsaturated chains can help prevent the bilayer becoming excessively ordered and rigid. Saturated chains may help maintain ordered structure at higher temperatures. This adaptation concerns the lipid mixture, not an individual lipid switching between saturated and unsaturated states.

Lake sturgeon (Acipenser fulvescens) inhabit temperate freshwater with cold overwintering periods. Cold acclimation is associated with a greater proportion of unsaturated phospholipid fatty acids and fewer saturated ones. Bent cis-unsaturated tails hinder close packing, helping membranes remain functional in the cold. This is a change in the lipid mixture, not an individual lipid switching its saturation.

Lower temperature reduces molecular motion and can cause lipid tails to pack more tightly, potentially impairing membrane-associated transport and enzyme activity. Increasing the proportion of cis-unsaturated fatty-acid tails can hinder close packing and support useful fluidity at low temperatures. Some organisms also adjust chain length and other lipid components in response to environmental conditions. This process, often called homeoviscous adaptation, is not the instantaneous action of a single membrane molecule: it involves biochemical regulation of membrane composition. A straight saturated tail and a cis-kinked unsaturated tail should be represented differently in diagrams. Be cautious about assuming that the same lipid change has identical effects in every type of membrane.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can one membrane component restrain excessive motion while preventing cold rigidity?
sections.explanation:
Cholesterol is an amphipathic sterol with a small polar hydroxyl group near phospholipid heads and a largely hydrophobic ring system inserted among fatty-acid tails. Its position matters: it is not a free aqueous solute or a pore.

At relatively high temperatures cholesterol can constrain lipid movement and reduce excessive permeability; at low temperatures it interrupts close packing and helps resist abrupt rigidification. Its net influence depends on temperature and lipid composition, so saying it simply increases fluidity in every context is wrong.

Animal plasma membranes often contain cholesterol as a fluidity modulator. The functional consequence is stability of membrane behaviour across varying conditions rather than turning the membrane into a solid sheet.

Cholesterol has a polar hydroxyl near the phospholipid head-group region and a rigid nonpolar ring system inserted between fatty-acid tails. At relatively high temperatures, the rigid rings can restrain certain tail movements; at lower temperatures, cholesterol can interfere with extremely tight phospholipid packing. As a result it can moderate changes in membrane physical properties over a useful temperature range in many animal cells. Its effect depends on lipid composition and temperature, so it is not scientifically accurate to say that cholesterol always increases fluidity or always decreases it. Plant and bacterial membranes have different sterol compositions and cannot be assumed to behave exactly like a typical animal plasma membrane.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can a continuous cell boundary surround cargo or release vesicle contents?
sections.explanation:
Membrane lipids can curve and reorganize, allowing small membrane-bound compartments to form and fuse. In endocytosis the plasma membrane invaginates, encloses material and pinches off into the cell. The material becomes separated from the cytosol by a vesicle membrane.

In exocytosis an intracellular vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing its lumenal contents to the exterior. The two processes move material by changing membrane topology rather than by pushing whole proteins through lipid tails. Cellular machinery and energy-dependent steps may be involved in actual vesicle traffic.

Receptor-mediated uptake of low-density lipoprotein particles exemplifies endocytosis; secretion of a peptide hormone exemplifies exocytosis. Fluidity makes membrane bending and fusion physically possible, but it is not sufficient alone to specify cargo or trigger fusion.

Endocytosis brings material into a cell by inward bending and pinching off part of the plasma membrane, creating a vesicle containing extracellular material. Exocytosis follows the opposite membrane-fusion event: a vesicle formed inside the cell merges with the plasma membrane so its lumen communicates with the exterior. The leaflet orientation is conserved, a key point for understanding where carbohydrate chains and protein domains appear after fusion. Endocytosis may be selective, as in receptor-mediated uptake, or involve larger volumes or particles in other pathways. Exocytosis can deliver both secreted molecules and additional membrane material. Neither process is equivalent to simple diffusion through the lipid core.

Exocytosis: secretion by membrane fusion

sections.guidingQuestion: What causes a specific neuronal ion channel to switch between closed and open states?
sections.explanation:
A gated ion channel switches accessibility in response to a defined signal. At a neuromuscular junction, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors bind acetylcholine on the extracellular side. Their opening permits cation flux, producing a depolarizing response in the muscle end plate under physiological conditions.

Voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels instead respond to changes in membrane potential. Their distinct activation and inactivation kinetics help shape an action potential: rapid Na+ permeability changes usually contribute to depolarization, while delayed K+ permeability contributes to repolarization.

Gating changes whether ions have a pathway; an open channel still permits movement only down the relevant electrochemical gradient. A neurotransmitter-gated receptor is not the same mechanism as a voltage sensor even if both can contribute to electrical signalling.

A ligand-gated ion channel changes opening probability when a chemical messenger binds, as at nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. A voltage-gated Na⁺ channel responds to changes in the electrical potential across the membrane. After either type opens, ions pass according to their electrochemical driving forces; the gating stimulus does not itself determine an uphill direction. In neurons, such channels contribute to changes in membrane potential and the propagation of electrical signals. Channels can also enter inactivated states, so 'ligand removed means fully open' and 'voltage change means permanently open' are not appropriate assumptions. Sketch a clearly separated gate, pore and direction of net ion movement.

terms: Ligand-gated channel: gated by molecular binding
Voltage-gated channel: gated by membrane voltage

sections.guidingQuestion: How does the Na+/K+-ATPase support a neuron's electrical conditions?
sections.explanation:
The animal Na+/K+-ATPase is an integral membrane exchange transporter that cycles through ion-binding conformations. For each ATP hydrolyzed, its typical physiological cycle exports three Na+ ions from the cytosol and imports two K+ ions. Both transport directions oppose prevailing electrochemical gradients.

This electrogenic exchange moves one net positive charge outward per cycle. It contributes directly to membrane potential and, crucially, maintains the Na+ and K+ gradients that channels exploit. Most immediate resting membrane potential is associated with permeability, notably to K+, so do not imply the pump alone creates the full resting potential.

During repeated nerve activity, gradients would gradually dissipate without pump action. The ATPase supports future excitability even though the rapid upstroke of an action potential results primarily from opening channels, not from a burst of pump cycles.

The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase typically exports three Na⁺ ions from the cytosol and imports two K⁺ ions for each ATP hydrolysed. Alternating binding affinity and conformational states ensure the ions move in the correct directions rather than through an open channel. This exchange is electrogenic because one net positive charge moves outward per cycle. The pump maintains Na⁺ and K⁺ gradients that support multiple cell functions, including the conditions from which neuronal resting potentials and action potentials arise. The resting potential itself also depends strongly on passive ion permeability, particularly K⁺ leak conductance; attributing the entire resting voltage directly to the pump would be misleading.
sections.revisionSummary: Per ATP: three Na+ out, two K+ in; electrogenic action and gradient maintenance support membrane potentials.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can an intestinal cell absorb glucose even when its glucose concentration is high?
sections.explanation:
A sodium-dependent glucose cotransporter binds Na+ and glucose on the same side of a membrane and alternates access to deliver both inward. The favourable electrochemical entry of Na+ supplies energy that can drive glucose uptake against its glucose concentration gradient. This is secondary or indirect active transport.

The Na+ gradient is maintained chiefly by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase using ATP. Therefore the cotransporter does not hydrolyze ATP directly in its transport step, but the overall process ultimately depends on ATP-powered gradient maintenance. Glucose can then leave the enterocyte across its basolateral membrane using an appropriate facilitated transporter when its gradient allows.

This arrangement enables glucose absorption by small-intestinal epithelial cells and reabsorption in proximal nephron tubules. Different SGLT isoforms differ in coupling ratio; do not label all sodium–glucose cotransporters with a single universal stoichiometry.

A sodium–glucose cotransporter on the apical membrane of an intestinal epithelial cell uses the favorable inward Na⁺ electrochemical gradient to move glucose into the cell, potentially against its own concentration gradient. The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase on the basolateral membrane consumes ATP to maintain low cytosolic Na⁺, indirectly supplying the energy that drives this coupled transport. Glucose can then leave through a basolateral facilitated-diffusion transporter when the glucose gradient favors export. The symporter itself is not an ATPase. The orientation of apical and basolateral surfaces matters: drawing the pump and symporter on the wrong membrane face reverses the physiological explanation.

sections.guidingQuestion: How can membranes help neighbouring cells form a coherent tissue?
sections.explanation:
Cell-adhesion molecules (CAMs) are cell-surface proteins that help cells attach to adjacent cells or relevant extracellular structures. By providing selective molecular recognition and physical links, CAMs help organize cells into tissues and maintain structural integrity.

Different intercellular junction types employ different adhesion proteins; the IB understanding requires this principle rather than a memorized catalogue of every protein or junction. CAM-mediated binding is not identical to fusion of adjacent plasma membranes. Adhesion often works with intracellular cytoskeletal linkages and tissue mechanics.

In epithelial tissue, cell-cell adhesion helps neighbouring cells remain connected as a continuous layer despite mechanical stresses. Defective adhesion can compromise tissue cohesion even while each individual cell's lipid bilayer remains intact.

Cell-adhesion proteins help neighboring cells recognize and remain connected, but different junctions have different mechanical and signaling roles. Cadherin-family proteins participate in adhesion between many animal cells; other components connect junctions to the cytoskeleton. Tight junctions help limit paracellular leakage in epithelia, while desmosomes provide stronger attachment in tissues exposed to mechanical strain. Gap junctions instead create pathways for small molecules and ions to communicate between neighboring cells. These complexes should not all be drawn as identical adhesive hooks. Stable tissue organization depends on the position and combination of junctions, enabling coordinated barriers, mechanical integrity and cell signaling.

Predicts weakening of the inward Na⁺ electrochemical gradient after prolonged inhibition.
Predicts reduced SGLT-mediated glucose uptake against its gradient on the apical membrane.
Explains that SGLT uses stored Na⁺ gradient energy indirectly rather than directly hydrolysing ATP (and GLUT cannot replace that coupling).

questions.prompt: Compare simple diffusion of oxygen, facilitated diffusion of K⁺ through an open channel, and ATP-powered pumping of an ion. For each route, state whether a transport protein is required, what determines its direction and whether the membrane transporter directly consumes ATP.
questions.answer: O₂ uses the bilayer without a protein and moves down its concentration gradient without ATP. K⁺ uses a selective channel, moves down its electrochemical gradient and does not require transport ATP. An ATPase pump binds ions and hydrolyses ATP, allowing movement against an electrochemical gradient.
markingPoints: Identify direct oxygen passage through bilayer without a transporter.
State simple diffusion moves down a concentration gradient without direct ATP use.
Identify selective channel as a protein facilitating ion movement.
State channel flux follows the electrochemical gradient without directly consuming transport ATP.
Explain ATP-dependent pump can transport ions against electrochemical gradient.

questions.prompt: An Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase completes 25 cycles with its usual physiological ion stoichiometry. Calculate the numbers of Na⁺ exported, K⁺ imported and net elementary positive charges transported outward, and explain the energy requirement.
questions.answer: 25 × 3 = 75 Na⁺ exported; 25 × 2 = 50 K⁺ imported; 75 − 50 = 25 elementary positive charges moved outward. Each cycle hydrolyses one ATP, so 25 ATP are used.
markingPoints: Calculate 75 Na⁺ exported.
Calculate 50 K⁺ imported.
Calculate a net of 25 elementary positive charges outward.
Explain 25 ATP hydrolyses fuel 25 normal cycles.

questions.prompt: A drug inhibits the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase of small-intestinal epithelial cells. Predict the longer-term effect on apical sodium–glucose uptake and explain the causal chain, including whether the SGLT directly hydrolyses ATP.
questions.answer: Pump inhibition allows intracellular Na⁺ to rise and weakens the electrochemical Na⁺ gradient. As the gradient dissipates, coupled apical Na⁺/glucose uptake becomes less energetically favourable and declines. SGLT uses Na⁺ gradient energy directly, not direct ATP hydrolysis; the pump's ATP use sustains that gradient.
markingPoints: Locate inhibited Na⁺/K⁺ pump on basolateral membrane.
Explain cytosolic Na⁺ accumulation or weakened Na⁺ electrochemical gradient over time.
Predict reduced apical glucose uptake as Na⁺-linked driving force declines.
Explain that SGLT couples downhill Na⁺ entry to glucose movement.
Distinguish indirect ATP dependence from direct ATP hydrolysis at SGLT.
